entries.1:1: This introduces Job as a genuinely good man who took God seriously and avoided doing wrong. It tells the reader that what follows is about a truly upright person, not someone being punished for hidden sins.
entries.1:2: Job had a large family of seven sons and three daughters. This shows he was blessed with children, which was seen as a great sign of God's favor.
entries.1:3: Job owned enormous herds and many servants, making him the richest man in that region. The reader should see that he had very much to lose.
entries.1:4: Job's sons took turns hosting feasts and always included their sisters. This shows a close, happy family that enjoyed being together.
entries.1:5: After each round of parties, Job offered sacrifices just in case his children had sinned in their hearts. He was a careful, loving father who looked out for his family's spiritual welfare.
entries.1:6: This scene shifts to a heavenly gathering where spiritual beings present themselves before God, and an accuser figure comes too. It lets the reader see behind the scenes of what is about to happen to Job.
entries.1:7: God asks the accuser where he has been, and he answers that he has been roaming around the earth. This shows the accuser as a restless wanderer looking over the world.
entries.1:8: God himself points to Job as an example of a truly good man, with no one else like him on earth. This tells the reader that Job's goodness is real and recognized by God himself.
entries.1:9: The accuser questions Job's motives, suggesting he only serves God for what he gets out of it. This raises the central question of whether people can be good without expecting rewards.
entries.1:10: The accuser points out that God has protected Job and made him prosper on every side. He implies that Job's devotion is bought by blessing, not genuine.
entries.1:11: The accuser challenges God to take away everything Job has and predicts Job will curse God openly. This sets up the test that will drive the whole story.
entries.1:12: God permits the accuser to destroy Job's possessions but forbids him to harm Job himself. The reader should see that the coming disasters are allowed by God but limited by him.
entries.1:13: The scene returns to earth on a day when Job's children were all together feasting at the oldest brother's house. This sets the stage for the tragedy that is about to strike.
entries.1:14: A messenger rushes in to Job while his oxen were plowing and donkeys were grazing nearby. This is the first of several rapid reports of disaster.
entries.1:15: Raiders from Sheba attacked and carried off the animals and killed the workers, with only this one man escaping. Job loses his livestock and servants in a single blow.
entries.1:16: Before the first messenger finished, another arrived saying fire from heaven burned up all the sheep and the workers. Job's losses are piling up faster than he can absorb.
entries.1:17: A third messenger reports that Chaldean raiders took all the camels and killed the servants. Job's wealth is being stripped away piece by piece.
entries.1:18: While the third messenger was still speaking, a fourth arrived with news about Job's children. The worst news is saved for last.
entries.1:19: A great wind collapsed the house where all his children were feasting, and they all died. Job has now lost not only his wealth but every one of his children.
entries.1:20: Job responds by tearing his clothes, shaving his head, and falling to the ground in worship. His grief is real and expressed openly, yet he turns toward God rather than away.
entries.1:21: Job says he came into the world with nothing and will leave with nothing, and that God gives and takes away. He accepts his losses and still praises God, showing remarkable faith.
entries.1:22: Despite everything, Job did not sin or accuse God of doing wrong. The reader is shown that Job's faith held up under the first great test.
entries.2:1: This scene shows a heavenly gathering where God meets with spiritual beings, and an accuser figure comes among them. It reminds the reader that unseen spiritual realities are at work behind human events.
entries.2:2: God asks the accuser where he has been, and he answers that he has been roaming the earth. This pictures an adversary who is active and watching in the world.
entries.2:3: God points to Job as a genuinely good and faithful man and notes that Job has stayed faithful even after losing so much for no reason. The reader is reminded that God sees and values real integrity.
entries.2:4: The accuser argues that people will give up anything, even others, to save their own lives. He is claiming Job's devotion is really just self-interest.
entries.2:5: The accuser says that if Job's own body is harmed, Job will openly curse God. He is betting that Job's faith will collapse under physical suffering.
entries.2:6: God allows the accuser to harm Job's body but sets a firm limit: Job's life must be spared. Even in severe testing, God keeps control and sets boundaries.
entries.2:7: The accuser strikes Job with a painful skin disease from head to foot. Job's suffering becomes even more personal and physical.
entries.2:8: Job sits among ashes and scrapes his sores with a piece of broken pottery. This shows how raw and humiliating his suffering had become.
entries.2:9: Job's wife urges him to curse God and die, essentially telling him to give up. Her words add emotional pain to his physical suffering.
entries.2:10: Job replies that if we accept good from God, we should also accept hardship, and he does not sin with his words. He shows steady faith without pretending life is fair.
entries.2:11: Three friends hear about Job's disaster and arrange to meet, coming from their homes to grieve with him and comfort him. Their willingness to show up is a picture of real friendship in hard times.
entries.2:12: When the friends see Job from a distance, they barely recognize him, and they weep and show signs of deep grief. Their reaction shows how shocking and severe Job's suffering was.
entries.2:13: The friends sit with Job on the ground for seven days and nights without saying anything, because they see how great his pain is. Sometimes the most caring thing a person can do is simply stay present and quiet with someone who is hurting.
entries.3:1: Job finally speaks, and the first thing he does is wish he had never been born. It shows how deep his pain has become, and that honest grief can be spoken out loud.
entries.3:2: This simply introduces Job's words: he opens his mouth and answers. It reminds the reader that what follows is Job speaking from his pain.
entries.3:3: Job wishes the day of his birth and the night he was conceived could be wiped out. He is saying his life feels like a mistake, not a gift.
entries.3:4: He asks that the day he was born be swallowed in darkness and ignored by God. It shows how completely he wants that day erased.
entries.3:5: He calls on darkness and thick clouds to claim that day and frighten it. The reader sees grief so heavy that even the calendar feels like an enemy.
entries.3:6: He wants that night to be forgotten, never counted among the days or months. It is his way of saying, let my existence leave no trace.
entries.3:7: He asks that the night be barren and silent, with no sound of celebration. He wants no joy attached to the memory of his coming into the world.
entries.3:8: He imagines people who curse days calling down a curse on that night, even waking a sea monster to do it. It shows how fiercely he wants that night destroyed.
entries.3:9: He wants the stars of that morning to go dark and the dawn never to arrive. Even the first light of his life should, in his wish, be blotted out.
entries.3:10: He blames that day for not closing his mother's womb, so trouble could have been kept from him. He is saying he wishes suffering had never reached him.
entries.3:11: He asks why he did not die the moment he was born. It is a raw question from someone who sees life as pain rather than gift.
entries.3:12: He wonders why he was held and fed as a baby instead of being allowed to die. He is questioning the care that kept him alive.
entries.3:13: He says that if he had died, he would now be resting quietly and sleeping in peace. Death looks to him like the only rest available.
entries.3:14: He imagines lying down with kings and wise rulers who built great houses. Even the mighty end in the same quiet place.
entries.3:15: He pictures being at rest with rich rulers whose houses were full of gold and silver. Wealth, he sees, does not prevent death.
entries.3:16: He wishes he had been a stillborn child who never saw light. It is a wish to have been spared awareness of suffering altogether.
entries.3:17: In the grave, he says, the wicked stop stirring and the exhausted finally rest. Death looks like the place where struggle ends.
entries.3:18: He imagines prisoners resting together with no overseer shouting at them. Even captives, he says, find peace in death.
entries.3:19: In that place small and great are alike, and servants are free from their masters. Death, to Job, erases all rank and bondage.
entries.3:20: He asks why God gives light and life to people who are miserable and bitter. It is a hard question about why suffering people keep living.
entries.3:21: He describes people who long for death but cannot find it, hunting for it like hidden treasure. He is naming a longing many in deep pain will recognize.
entries.3:22: Such people, he says, would rejoice and be glad when they finally reach the grave. For Job, death feels like relief rather than loss.
entries.3:23: He asks why life is given to a man whose path is hidden and whom God has fenced in. He feels trapped by God and unable to see a way forward.
entries.3:24: Instead of food he has grief, and his sorrow pours out like water. His pain is constant and physical, not just a mood.
entries.3:25: He says the very thing he feared has come upon him, and his heart is shaken. It shows how dread and loss have overtaken him.
entries.3:26: He has no peace, no quiet, no rest, only trouble pressing in. It is a plain statement of how completely his suffering has taken over.
entries.4:1: Eliphaz, one of Job's friends, speaks up to answer him. This begins the first of the friends' speeches that will push back against Job's complaints.
entries.4:2: Eliphaz asks whether Job would be offended if someone said a word, yet he feels he cannot hold back what he is thinking. He is politely but firmly preparing to challenge Job.
entries.4:3: Eliphaz admits that Job has helped many people and strengthened those who were weak. He is acknowledging Job's good past before making his point.
entries.4:4: Job's words used to lift up people who were stumbling and give strength to those who were giving way. Eliphaz is reminding Job of the encouragement he once gave others.
entries.4:5: But now trouble has hit Job himself, and he is worn down and shaken by it. Eliphaz is pointing out that Job is not handling hardship the way he once helped others to.
entries.4:6: Eliphaz asks whether Job's reverence for God and his honest life are not what should give him confidence and hope. He is suggesting Job should trust his own good record.
entries.4:7: Eliphaz asks Job to think of any example where an honest, God-fearing person was ever destroyed. He is implying that bad things only happen to bad people.
entries.4:8: From what Eliphaz has seen, people who cause trouble and plant evil end up reaping the same trouble for themselves. He is stating his belief that people get what they deserve.
entries.4:9: Such people are destroyed by God's breath and swept away by the wind of his anger. Eliphaz is saying God himself brings down those who do evil.
entries.4:10: Even if a lion roars loudly and shows its teeth, those teeth get broken. Eliphaz uses this picture to say that even the strong and fierce are brought down.
entries.4:11: The old lion starves for lack of food, and the young lions scatter with nowhere to go. The point is that even the mightiest creatures can end up with nothing.
entries.4:12: Eliphaz says a message was quietly given to him and he caught its faint sound. He is setting up a claim that his insight came from a special revelation.
entries.4:13: This happened at night during troubling dreams, when people are deep in sleep. He is describing a nighttime vision that left him shaken.
entries.4:14: Fear and trembling came over him, and his whole body felt disturbed. The experience was frightening, not comforting.
entries.4:15: A breath moved across his face, and the hair on his body stood up. He is describing an eerie, physical sense of something supernatural near him.
entries.4:16: Something stood before him that he could not quite make out, and then a quiet voice spoke. The voice is about to deliver the message Eliphaz wants Job to hear.
entries.4:17: The voice asks whether a mere human can be truly right or clean before God. The implied answer is no, and Eliphaz is using this to argue that no person can claim innocence.
entries.4:18: God does not fully trust even his own servants, and he finds fault even in angels. Eliphaz is saying that if even heavenly beings fall short, humans surely do too.
entries.4:19: How much more, then, are people who live in fragile bodies made of dust, easily crushed like a bug. Eliphaz is stressing how small and weak humans are compared to God.
entries.4:20: People can be broken from morning to evening and die unnoticed, gone forever. He is saying human life is brief and easily ended.
entries.4:21: When the tent rope is pulled up, they die, and they die without having gained wisdom. Eliphaz ends his vision by saying people are taken down before they truly understand.
entries.5:1: Eliphaz dares Job to call for help and asks which heavenly being would bother answering him. It means Job should not expect any angel to take his side.
entries.5:2: Resentment and hot temper destroy a foolish person, and someone without wisdom ruins himself by his own passion. It warns the reader that unchecked anger and envy tear a person down.
entries.5:3: Eliphaz says he has watched foolish people seem to succeed and settle down, only to have disaster strike their home suddenly. It reminds the reader that a secure-looking life can collapse without warning.
entries.5:4: The foolish man's children have no one to protect them and are crushed in court because nobody defends their case. It means the harm a person does can fall on his family, who are left helpless.
entries.5:5: Hungry strangers and thirsty people take the foolish man's crops and water, so his wealth ends up feeding others. It pictures how quickly a person's goods can be stripped away and given to those in need.
entries.5:6: Trouble does not just sprout up on its own out of the ground like a weed. It means hardship has a cause and does not come from nowhere.
entries.5:7: Just as sparks fly upward from a fire, so trouble is bound to come to people from birth. It tells the reader that suffering is a normal part of human life, not a strange accident.
entries.5:8: Eliphaz says that if he were in Job's place, he would bring his case to God and lay it out before him. It means the right response to trouble is to turn to God rather than argue with people.
entries.5:9: God does great things we cannot understand and countless wonders. It reminds the reader that God's work is far beyond what we can grasp.
entries.5:10: God sends rain on the land and waters the fields. It means the ordinary gifts of nature, like rain, are signs of God's care.
entries.5:11: God lifts up those who are brought low and puts sorrowful people in a safe place. It gives hope that God notices the humble and the hurting.
entries.5:12: God frustrates the plans of clever people so their schemes fail. It means human cleverness cannot outsmart God's purposes.
entries.5:13: God catches the wise in their own tricks and brings the plans of crooked people to a sudden end. It warns that scheming against others eventually backfires.
entries.5:14: Those clever schemers stumble around in broad daylight as if it were night. It means their own confusion leaves them helpless when they thought they were in control.
entries.5:15: God rescues the fatherless and the poor from the sword and from the grip of the powerful. It assures the reader that God stands with those who have no one to defend them.
entries.5:16: So the poor have hope, and wrongdoing is silenced. It means God's justice gives the weak something to hope for and shuts down the boastful.
entries.5:17: The person God corrects is truly happy, so do not refuse his discipline. It means hard lessons from God are a sign of care, not rejection.
entries.5:18: God wounds, but he also bandages; he punishes, but his hands also heal. It means God's correction is not the end of the story, because he restores afterward.
entries.5:19: God will rescue you from six troubles, and even a seventh will not harm you. It means God's protection covers trouble after trouble, not just one crisis.
entries.5:20: In famine God keeps you from death, and in war he keeps you from the sword. It means God can preserve a person through the worst kinds of danger.
entries.5:21: God will protect you from harmful words and from ruin when it comes. It means you need not fear gossip or disaster, because God is your shield.
entries.5:22: You will laugh at destruction and hunger and have no fear of wild animals. It means trust in God can make a person bold even in frightening circumstances.
entries.5:23: You will be at peace with the stones of the field and with the wild animals. It pictures a life where even nature works with you instead of against you.
entries.5:24: You will know your home is at peace and find nothing missing when you check your property. It means a settled, secure household is part of God's blessing.
entries.5:25: You will know your family will be many, like plants growing across the land. It means God's blessing includes a flourishing future for your descendants.
entries.5:26: You will come to your grave at a ripe old age, like grain gathered at harvest time. It means a full, long life and a peaceful death are God's gift.
entries.5:27: Eliphaz says they have carefully examined all this and found it true, so Job should take it to heart. It means he is urging Job to accept his advice as reliable, though Job must weigh it for himself.
entries.6:1: Job speaks up in reply to his friend's criticism. He is about to defend himself and explain how he feels.
entries.6:2: Job wishes his grief could be weighed on a scale so everyone could see how heavy it really is. He wants his friends to understand that his pain is enormous.
entries.6:3: He says his sorrow would outweigh all the sand of the sea, which is why his words have been wild and rash. His heavy pain explains his reckless speech.
entries.6:4: Job feels God has shot him with arrows and filled him with terror, like an army lined up against him. He believes God himself is the source of his suffering.
entries.6:5: A donkey doesn't bray when it has grass, and an ox doesn't complain when it has food. In the same way, Job says, people only cry out when they truly have reason to.
entries.6:6: Food with no salt has no taste, and the white of an egg has no flavor. Job is saying that tasteless things are not worth eating, just as his friends' words bring him no comfort.
entries.6:7: Job refuses to touch such tasteless food; to him it is like sickening stuff. He is saying his whole situation has become repulsive to him.
entries.6:8: Job longs for God to answer his prayer and give him what he asks for. He is desperate for some response from God.
entries.6:9: Job wishes God would just end his life and crush him. He would rather die than keep suffering like this.
entries.6:10: Even in dying, Job would have one comfort: he has not denied the words of the Holy One. He holds on to his integrity even while wishing for death.
entries.6:11: Job asks what strength he has left to keep waiting, and what future he has to hope for. He feels he cannot endure much longer.
entries.6:12: Job asks whether he is made of stone or bronze, meaning he is not unfeeling or superhuman. He is a fragile human being with limits to what he can bear.
entries.6:13: Job says he has no help left in himself and no wisdom to draw on. He feels completely empty and helpless.
entries.6:14: A person who refuses kindness to a suffering friend has stopped fearing God. Job is saying his friends are failing a basic duty of loyalty.
entries.6:15: Job compares his friends to a stream that dries up, deceiving travelers who counted on it. They have proven unreliable when he needed them most.
entries.6:16: Such streams look full because of ice and snow that feed them. They seem promising at first, just as his friends seemed supportive at first.
entries.6:17: When the hot weather comes, the stream dries up and disappears. In the same way, his friends vanished when his trouble got hot.
entries.6:18: Caravans turn aside to find water but end up wandering into empty land and dying. People who trusted the stream are ruined by its failure.
entries.6:19: Traders from Tema and Sheba searched carefully and waited for water. They counted on the stream to save them.
entries.6:20: They were disappointed and ashamed because their hope failed. Job's friends have disappointed him the same way.
entries.6:21: Job tells his friends they have become like that dried-up stream to him; they see his terrible condition and are afraid. Their fear has made them useless to him.
entries.6:22: Job asks whether he ever begged them for money or asked them to pay a debt for him. He never asked them for anything costly.
entries.6:23: He never asked them to rescue him from an enemy or buy his freedom from cruel people. He only wanted their support, not their money.
entries.6:24: Job invites them to teach him and he will be silent, and to show him where he has gone wrong. He is willing to listen if they have real answers.
entries.6:25: Honest words are pleasant to hear, but Job asks what their arguments actually prove. Their scolding carries no real weight.
entries.6:26: Job says they treat his words as mere wind, the empty talk of a hopeless man. They dismiss him instead of answering him.
entries.6:27: Job accuses them of being willing to trade away a helpless orphan and even to bargain over a friend. He feels they are treating him like something to be sold.
entries.6:28: Job asks them to look him in the eye, because he will not lie to their faces. He wants them to see he is speaking honestly.
entries.6:29: Job urges them to change their minds and stop judging him wrongly, because he is still in the right. He asks them to reconsider their harsh opinion of him.
entries.6:30: Job asks whether there is any evil in what he says, and whether he doesn't clearly know his own trouble. He insists he understands his situation and is not speaking wickedness.
entries.7:1: Job is saying that human life on earth is like hard labor, with trouble assigned to us and days spent like a hired worker waiting for pay. It reminds the reader that suffering is a normal part of life, not always a sign that something is uniquely wrong with you.
entries.7:2: A servant longs for the cool evening and a worker waits for his wages, just as people long for relief from their labor. The reader can see that longing for rest and reward is a natural human feeling.
entries.7:3: Job says his inheritance has been empty months of pain and nights of exhausting weariness. He is describing his suffering honestly, showing the reader that it is okay to name how hard life feels.
entries.7:4: When Job lies down, he wonders when it will be time to get up, and the night drags on while he tosses and turns until dawn. This captures the misery of sleepless nights and the feeling that time moves painfully slowly when you are suffering.
entries.7:5: Job describes his body as covered with worms and dirt, with skin that crusts over and then cracks open again. He is expressing how completely his illness has worn him down, body and spirit.
entries.7:6: Job says his days fly by faster than a weaver's thread and end without any hope. He feels his life is short and slipping away with nothing good to look forward to.
entries.7:7: Job asks God to remember that his life is like a breath, and he believes he will never see good again. He is pleading to be noticed in his pain, showing how deep despair can feel.
entries.7:8: Job says that once he is gone, no one will see him anymore, and even God's eyes will search for him but he will be gone. He is expressing the fear that death ends everything and that he will be forgotten.
entries.7:9: Just as a cloud disappears and never returns, Job says a person who goes down to the grave does not come back up. He is voicing the finality of death as he understands it.
entries.7:10: Job says the dead person never returns home, and his place no longer knows him. This shows his sense of being cut off from life and from everything familiar.
entries.7:11: Job decides he will not stay silent but will pour out his bitter feelings and complain in the pain of his spirit. The reader learns that honest, raw prayer to God is allowed, even when it sounds like complaint.
entries.7:12: Job asks God whether he is a sea or a sea monster that needs to be guarded and restrained. He feels God is watching him too closely, as if he were a dangerous force to be contained.
entries.7:13: Job thinks that lying in bed might bring him comfort and rest from his sickness. He is looking for even a small relief from his suffering.
entries.7:14: But instead of rest, God sends frightening dreams and terrifying visions. Job feels that even sleep offers him no escape from fear.
entries.7:15: Job says he would rather be strangled to death than keep living with his pain. This shows how extreme his suffering has become and how honestly he expresses it.
entries.7:16: Job says he has no desire to live and does not want to live forever, asking God to leave him alone because his days are like a breath. He is worn out and wants his suffering to end.
entries.7:17: Job asks what a human being is that God would make him so important and keep such close attention on him. He is puzzled and overwhelmed that God seems so focused on him.
entries.7:18: Job says God checks on him every morning and tests him every moment. He feels constantly examined and watched, with no relief.
entries.7:19: Job asks how long it will be before God looks away and gives him even a moment to breathe. He is begging for a small break from the pressure he feels.
entries.7:20: Job asks that if he has sinned, what has he done to God, the watcher of people, and why God has made him a target so that he is a burden to himself. He is questioning why his suffering feels so personal and unrelenting.
entries.7:21: Job asks why God does not just forgive his sin and remove his guilt, since he will soon be dead and God will search for him but he will be gone. He is longing for forgiveness and relief before his life ends.
entries.8:1: Bildad, one of Job's friends, speaks up to answer him. This begins a speech from someone trying to explain Job's suffering.
entries.8:2: Bildad accuses Job of talking too much and letting his words blow around like empty wind. He is saying Job's defense of himself sounds like noise rather than truth.
entries.8:3: Bildad asks whether God ever makes unfair decisions or judges wrongly. He assumes God is always fair, which means Job's suffering must be deserved.
entries.8:4: Bildad claims that if Job's children sinned, their death was God's just punishment. He offers this as an explanation for Job's loss, though it adds to Job's pain.
entries.8:5: Bildad tells Job to earnestly seek God and pray to him. He thinks Job's problem is that he hasn't turned to God properly.
entries.8:6: Bildad promises that if Job is pure and honest, God will defend him and restore his home. He treats suffering as something you can fix by being good enough.
entries.8:7: Bildad says that even if Job's beginnings were small, God would make his future great. He is offering hope, but only on the condition that Job is innocent.
entries.8:8: Bildad urges Job to ask older generations and learn from what they discovered. He appeals to tradition as the reliable source of wisdom.
entries.8:9: Bildad admits that people live only a short time and know very little. He uses this to argue that Job should listen to the wisdom of those who came before.
entries.8:10: Bildad says the older generations will teach Job and share their wisdom with him. He expects their words to correct Job's thinking.
entries.8:11: Bildad uses a picture of a river plant that needs wet ground to grow. He is saying that nothing thrives without the right conditions, just as no one succeeds without God.
entries.8:12: The plant dries up and dies while still green, before it is even cut. Bildad means that people who forget God can collapse suddenly, even when things look fine.
entries.8:13: Bildad says this is what happens to everyone who forgets God, and that the wicked person's hope dies. He is warning Job that ignoring God leads to ruin.
entries.8:14: Bildad says the wicked person's confidence is cut off and his hope is as flimsy as a spider's web. He means that trusting in anything other than God will fail.
entries.8:15: The wicked man leans on his family and home for security, but they cannot save him. Bildad is saying that earthly things give no real support when trouble comes.
entries.8:16: Bildad pictures a wicked man thriving in the sunshine with branches spreading over his garden. He describes how prosperous and secure such a person can look for a time.
entries.8:17: The wicked man's roots wrap around rocks and push into crevices, seeming firmly planted. Bildad is describing someone who looks deeply established and hard to remove.
entries.8:18: Yet if that person is pulled from his place, it acts as if it never knew him. Bildad means that a wicked person's success can vanish and be forgotten quickly.
entries.8:19: Bildad says this is the short-lived joy of the wicked man's path, and someone else soon takes his place. He is stressing that evil success does not last.
entries.8:20: Bildad insists that God will not abandon a blameless person or support evildoers. He is confident that God always rewards good and punishes bad, which is his main point against Job.
entries.8:21: Bildad promises that God will yet fill Job's mouth with laughter and shouts of joy. He is offering Job a hopeful outcome if Job turns out to be innocent.
entries.8:22: Bildad says Job's enemies will be covered with shame and the wicked person's home will disappear. He ends by predicting that Job's troubles will reverse and his opponents will be disgraced.
entries.9:1: Job begins his reply to his friend. He is about to answer what was just said to him.
entries.9:2: Job agrees that God is just, but asks how any ordinary person could ever prove themselves right in front of God. It means we can't win an argument with God on our own.
entries.9:3: If someone tried to argue their case with God, they couldn't answer even one question out of a thousand. God knows far more than we do.
entries.9:4: God is deeply wise and very powerful, and no one who has fought against him has ever come out ahead. It's foolish to think we can resist God and win.
entries.9:5: God can move or remove mountains without anyone even noticing, and he does it in his anger. Nothing in creation is too big for him to overturn.
entries.9:6: God can shake the earth out of its place so that even its foundations tremble. The whole world is under his control.
entries.9:7: God can command the sun to stop shining and the stars to go dark. Even the sky obeys his orders.
entries.9:8: God stretched out the heavens and walks on the waves of the sea. He rules over everything above and below.
entries.9:9: God made the constellations—the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades—and the far southern skies. He is the maker of all the stars.
entries.9:10: God does great things we can't figure out and wonders too many to count. We should be humble before a God like that.
entries.9:11: God can pass right by us and we won't even see or notice him. He is at work whether we are aware of it or not.
entries.9:12: If God decides to take something away, no one can stop him or ask him what he's doing. He has the right to do as he pleases.
entries.9:13: God's anger can't be turned aside, and even the strongest helpers were crushed under him. No power can stand against God.
entries.9:14: So how could Job possibly argue his case or find the right words to answer God? We are far too small to debate with him.
entries.9:15: Even if Job were in the right, he couldn't answer God; he could only beg for mercy from the one who seems to be against him. Being right doesn't guarantee winning with God.
entries.9:16: Even if God came when Job called, Job wouldn't be sure God would listen to him. It feels to him like God may not hear.
entries.9:17: Job feels God would crush him with a storm and multiply his wounds for no reason. He feels overwhelmed by suffering he didn't deserve.
entries.9:18: Job feels God won't even let him catch his breath, but fills him with bitter grief. His suffering feels constant and suffocating.
entries.9:19: If it comes down to strength, God is far stronger; if it comes to a legal case, no one can make God show up for trial. We can't force God to answer us.
entries.9:20: Even if Job were right, God would declare him wrong; even if innocent, God would call him guilty. Job feels he can never win.
entries.9:21: Job insists he is innocent, but he no longer cares what happens to him and has lost his will to live. Deep suffering can make life feel pointless.
entries.9:22: Job says it makes no difference to him—God destroys both the guilty and the innocent alike. It feels to him like good and bad people meet the same fate.
entries.9:23: When disaster strikes suddenly, Job feels God laughs at the suffering of innocent people. He is expressing raw pain, not a settled belief about God.
entries.9:24: Job says the world is handed over to wicked people and its judges are blinded; if God isn't behind it, then who is? He is wrestling with why evil seems to win.
entries.9:25: Job's days run by faster than a runner and vanish without any good coming to him. Life feels short and empty of hope.
entries.9:26: His days rush past like fast boats or an eagle swooping down on its prey. Time is slipping away quickly.
entries.9:27: Job considers trying to forget his grief, put on a happy face, and cheer up. He thinks about trying to move on.
entries.9:28: But he is still afraid of all his pain, certain that God will not treat him as innocent. Fear keeps pulling him back down.
entries.9:29: Job feels God will never clear him, so he wonders why he should bother trying at all. When you feel condemned no matter what, effort seems pointless.
entries.9:30: Even if Job washed himself with snow water and scrubbed his hands with soap, it wouldn't help. He feels no amount of cleansing could make him acceptable.
entries.9:31: Job feels God would still push him into the mud until even his clothes were disgusted with him. He feels utterly unclean and rejected.
entries.9:32: God isn't a man like Job, so Job can't answer him or meet him in court as an equal. There's a huge gap between God and us.
entries.9:33: There is no neutral judge between Job and God who could lay a hand on both of them. Job feels he has no one to settle the dispute fairly.
entries.9:34: Job wishes God would take away his punishing rod and stop terrifying him. He longs to be free from fear of God's punishment.
entries.9:35: Then Job would speak his mind without fear of God, because he doesn't believe he deserves this fear. He wants to speak freely without being crushed.
entries.10:1: Job is so worn down by suffering that he no longer wants to live, and he decides to stop holding back and pour out his bitter feelings in words. It shows that honest grief can be spoken out loud, even when it sounds raw.
entries.10:2: Job speaks directly to God, asking him not to treat him as guilty without showing him what he is being charged with. It reflects the pain of feeling accused and not knowing why.
entries.10:3: Job asks whether God gains anything by being harsh toward the work he himself made, while seeming to favor those who do wrong. It voices the confusion of someone who feels God is against him unfairly.
entries.10:4: Job asks whether God sees and judges the way a human being does, limited by human eyes. He is appealing to the idea that God must see more truly than people do.
entries.10:5: Job asks whether God's life is as short as a human's, so that he has to hurry to catch wrongdoing. He is questioning why God seems to be pressing him so hard and so quickly.
entries.10:6: Job suggests that God is hunting for his sin and keeping close track of any wrong he might do. It expresses the feeling of being watched and examined without mercy.
entries.10:7: Job insists that he is not a wrongdoer, yet no one can rescue him from God's power. He feels trapped between his innocence and God's seeming hostility.
entries.10:8: Job points out that God made him with his own hands, yet now seems to have turned against him and is tearing him down. It is the painful question of why the maker would destroy what he made.
entries.10:9: Job asks God to remember that he was formed from dust, and pleads that he not be sent back to dust so soon. He is asking for mercy based on how fragile he is.
entries.10:10: Job pictures his own beginning in the womb as something like milk being poured out and thickened into cheese. He is describing how God carefully formed him from soft, formless material.
entries.10:11: Job describes how God gave him skin, flesh, bones, and muscles, knitting him together piece by piece. He is acknowledging that his whole body is God's careful work.
entries.10:12: Job remembers that God showed him kindness, kept him alive by grace, and watched over his spirit. Even in his pain, he admits that his life has been sustained by God's care.
entries.10:13: Job believes God had a hidden plan all along, keeping these thoughts secret in his heart. He is struggling with the feeling that God's kindness was hiding something harder underneath.
entries.10:14: Job suspects that God was watching for any wrong he did and would never let him off the hook. It shows how exhausting it feels to live under constant suspicion.
entries.10:15: Job says that if he is guilty, he is doomed, and if he is innocent, he still cannot hold his head up because he is overwhelmed with shame and trouble. He feels there is no way to win.
entries.10:16: Job imagines that if he showed any strength or pride, God would hunt him like a lion and keep showing his power against him. He feels constantly targeted and overpowered.
entries.10:17: Job feels that God keeps bringing new charges and fresh attacks against him, as if sending one army after another. It describes the sense of being worn down by wave after wave of trouble.
entries.10:18: Job asks why he was even born, saying it would have been better to die at birth and never be seen. He is expressing deep despair about his existence.
entries.10:19: Job wishes he had gone straight from the womb to the grave, as though he had never existed. It is a cry of someone who feels his life has brought only pain.
entries.10:20: Job asks God to look away from him for a moment, since his life is short, so he can have a little relief. He is pleading for a brief break from constant scrutiny and suffering.
entries.10:21: Job is thinking about the grave, the place he will not return from, a land of darkness and gloom. He is facing the nearness of death and the sadness of it.
entries.10:22: Job describes the grave as a land of deep darkness and confusion, where even the light is dark. It shows how bleak and hopeless death feels to him in his suffering.
entries.11:1: Zophar from Naamah speaks up as the third friend to answer Job. This marks a new voice joining the argument.
entries.11:2: Zophar asks whether Job's many words should go unchallenged and whether talking a lot proves someone is right. He is accusing Job of assuming he is correct just because he talks so much.
entries.11:3: He asks whether Job's boastful talk should silence everyone and whether Job can mock without anyone correcting him. He thinks Job is being arrogant and needs to be called out.
entries.11:4: Zophar quotes Job's claim that his conduct is pure and he is innocent before God. He is setting up his argument against Job's insistence on his own innocence.
entries.11:5: Zophar wishes God would speak directly and argue with Job. He believes God's words would settle the matter against Job.
entries.11:6: He wishes God would reveal the hidden depths of wisdom, showing that God's purposes are beyond what Job understands. He hints that God may be punishing Job less than he deserves.
entries.11:7: Zophar asks whether Job can fully understand God or grasp the limits of the Almighty. The point is that God is far beyond human understanding.
entries.11:8: God's wisdom is higher than the heavens and deeper than the grave, beyond Job's reach. Zophar is saying Job cannot possibly figure God out.
entries.11:9: God's wisdom is longer than the earth and wider than the sea. It is far too vast for any person to measure.
entries.11:10: If God moves to arrest someone or bring them to death, no one can stop him. Zophar is stressing that God's power cannot be resisted.
entries.11:11: God sees through people and notices evil without effort. Nothing wicked escapes his attention.
entries.11:12: Zophar says a foolish person will gain wisdom only when a wild donkey is born tame, meaning it will never happen. He is calling Job foolish and hopeless to change on his own.
entries.11:13: Zophar tells Job to set his heart right and reach out to God in prayer. He is offering Job a way to fix his situation.
entries.11:14: He says Job must remove any wrongdoing from his hands and not let evil stay in his home. Repentance, in Zophar's view, is the condition for things to improve.
entries.11:15: Then Job could lift his face without shame and stand firm without fear. Zophar promises confidence and security if Job cleans up his life.
entries.11:16: Job would forget his troubles as water flows away. The pain of the past would fade from memory.
entries.11:17: Job's life would become brighter than noon, and even darkness would turn into morning. Zophar pictures a complete turnaround from gloom to light.
entries.11:18: Job would feel safe because there is hope, and he could rest peacefully after looking around. Security and calm would return to his life.
entries.11:19: Job would lie down without fear of danger, and people would seek his favor. He would be respected and at peace.
entries.11:20: But the wicked will wear out their eyes looking for help, find no escape, and have only death to hope for. Zophar ends by warning that evil people come to ruin.
entries.12:1: Job begins his reply to his friends. He is about to answer what they just said to him.
entries.12:2: Job says this sarcastically: his friends act as if they know everything and are the only wise people left. It warns the reader against being smug about having all the answers.
entries.12:3: Job insists he understands as much as they do and is not inferior to them. His point is that the obvious truths they keep repeating are things everyone already knows.
entries.12:4: Job feels like a joke to his neighbors, even though he prays to God and has lived uprightly. It shows that being mocked does not mean a person has done wrong.
entries.12:5: People who are comfortable look down on those who are struggling, as if trouble were always the sufferer's own fault. The reader is cautioned against contempt for people who are hurting.
entries.12:6: Job observes that those who do violence and provoke God often live securely and prosper. This is his honest complaint that life does not always reward the good and punish the bad.
entries.12:7: Job tells his friends to learn from animals and birds. Even creatures can teach a lesson about who really controls life.
entries.12:8: He extends the invitation to creatures that crawl on the ground and to fish in the sea. The whole created world can tell the same story if people will pay attention.
entries.12:9: Anyone can see from all these creatures that the Lord's hand made and governs them. Creation itself points to God's power.
entries.12:10: Every living creature's life and every human breath are held in God's hand. The reader can take comfort that life itself rests with God, not with chance.
entries.12:11: Just as the mouth tastes food, the ear tests what it hears. Job is saying his friends should weigh his words fairly instead of dismissing them.
entries.12:12: People assume that age brings wisdom and long life brings understanding. Job states this common belief before going on to qualify it.
entries.12:13: Real wisdom and strength belong to God, and power and understanding are his. Human wisdom is not the final authority.
entries.12:14: What God tears down cannot be rebuilt, and no one can release whom God shuts in. God's decisions are not overturned by human effort.
entries.12:15: God can hold back the waters so land dries up, or release them so the earth is flooded. He has authority over nature itself.
entries.12:16: Strength and sound judgment are with God, and both the deceiver and the deceived are in his hands. Nothing, not even error, escapes his control.
entries.12:17: God can strip advisers of their wisdom and make judges look foolish. Human expertise is not guaranteed to succeed.
entries.12:18: God can remove kings' authority and bind them instead. Earthly rulers are not beyond his reach.
entries.12:19: God can bring priests to ruin and overturn those who seemed securely established. Position and status offer no protection from him.
entries.12:20: God can silence trusted spokesmen and take away the good judgment of elders. Even respected voices can be shown to be wrong.
entries.12:21: God humbles leaders and removes power from the strong. Strength and rank do not impress him.
entries.12:22: God brings hidden things out of darkness and makes deep shadows bright. Nothing is too obscure for him to see or reveal.
entries.12:23: God can make nations great and then bring them down, expanding peoples and then dispersing them. The rise and fall of nations is in his hands.
entries.12:24: God can take away the understanding of the earth's rulers and leave them wandering in trackless waste. Leaders can be left without direction when God removes their insight.
entries.12:25: Such rulers grope in darkness with no light and stagger like drunkards with no one to help. It pictures how helpless human leaders become without God's guidance.
entries.13:1: Job is saying he has seen and heard these things for himself, so he really knows what he is talking about. It reminds the reader that personal experience can give real understanding.
entries.13:2: Job tells his friends that he understands as much as they do and is not beneath them. It means the reader should not assume someone who is suffering is ignorant or foolish.
entries.13:3: Job would rather speak directly to God and argue his case with him than keep debating with his friends. It shows that bringing honest questions straight to God is allowed.
entries.13:4: Job accuses his friends of covering up the truth and offering help that does not actually help. It warns the reader that comfort given with false or careless words does no good.
entries.13:5: Job says his friends would show more wisdom by staying silent. It means sometimes saying nothing is wiser than speaking.
entries.13:6: Job asks his friends to listen carefully to his argument and weigh his words. It shows he wants a fair hearing rather than being dismissed.
entries.13:7: Job asks whether they will speak wrongly on God's behalf and put false words in his mouth. It warns against defending God with lies or unfair claims.
entries.13:8: Job asks if they will show favoritism toward God and act as his defenders in this case. It means being partial in an argument is not the same as being right.
entries.13:9: Job asks whether it will go well for them when God examines them, since they cannot trick God like a man. It reminds the reader that God sees through our pretense.
entries.13:10: Job says God will correct them if they secretly show favoritism. It means hidden bias will not escape God's notice.
entries.13:11: Job asks whether God's greatness and fear should not make them tremble. It means God's majesty should make us humble and careful in what we say.
entries.13:12: Job calls their wise sayings dust and their defenses mere earth, meaning they are weak and worthless. It warns against trusting in impressive but empty words.
entries.13:13: Job tells them to be quiet and let him speak, whatever happens to him as a result. It shows his honesty and courage to speak his mind.
entries.13:14: Job says he will risk his own body and life to make his case. It means he is willing to take a real risk for the sake of honesty.
entries.13:15: Even if God kills him, Job says he will still argue his case before him and not back down. It shows remarkable trust that keeps talking to God even in despair.
entries.13:16: Job believes this bold approach will actually save him, because a wicked person would not dare come before God. It means honesty before God is safer than hiding.
entries.13:17: Job asks them to listen closely and store up his words in their minds. It means pay careful attention to what someone is really saying.
entries.13:18: Job says he has prepared his case and is confident he will be proven right. It shows his firm belief in his own innocence.
entries.13:19: Job asks if anyone can argue against him, because if so he would be silent and die. It means he is so sure of his case that he stakes his life on it.
entries.13:20: Job asks God for just two things before he comes to speak with him. It shows he is setting terms for a direct conversation with God.
entries.13:21: Job asks God to stop punishing him and to stop terrifying him with fear. It means he wants to talk freely without being overwhelmed.
entries.13:22: Job offers God a choice: God can call and Job will answer, or Job can speak and God can reply. It shows Job wants a real two-way conversation.
entries.13:23: Job asks God to tell him exactly what his wrongdoings and sins are. It means he wants to know the specific charge against him.
entries.13:24: Job asks why God hides his face and treats him like an enemy. It expresses the pain of feeling abandoned by God.
entries.13:25: Job asks if God will keep chasing something as weak as a leaf blown by the wind or a dry stick. It means he feels God is being harsh with someone already fragile.
entries.13:26: Job says God records bitter charges against him and makes him pay for the sins of his youth. It shows how past mistakes can feel like they are still being held against us.
entries.13:27: Job says God puts his feet in chains, watches all his paths, and limits his steps. It means he feels trapped and closely watched with no freedom.
entries.13:28: Job describes a person wearing away like rotten wood or a moth-eaten robe. It pictures how suffering makes a person feel worn down and fragile.
entries.14:1: Human life is brief and filled with hardship. This reminds the reader that trouble is a normal part of being human, not a sign that something is uniquely wrong with them.
entries.14:2: A person appears briefly like a flower and then is gone, fading like a shadow. It means our time is short, so life should be taken seriously.
entries.14:3: Job asks God why he would closely watch and judge a creature as weak and fleeting as a human being. It expresses the feeling that God's scrutiny seems too heavy for someone so fragile.
entries.14:4: A person who is already unclean cannot produce something clean on their own. It means we cannot fix our own moral brokenness by ourselves.
entries.14:5: God has set a fixed number of days and months for each person, with a limit they cannot pass. It means our lifespan is in God's hands, not fully under our control.
entries.14:6: Job asks God to look away and leave him alone so he can enjoy his short life like a hired worker who looks forward to his pay. It is a plea for relief from constant pressure.
entries.14:7: A tree that is cut down still has hope of growing again. This sets up a contrast: nature can recover, but humans seem not to.
entries.14:8: Even when a tree's root is old and its stump is dead in the ground, there is still hope. It means apparent death is not always the end for a tree.
entries.14:9: Just a little water makes the stump sprout and grow like a young plant. It shows how quickly life can return when conditions are right.
entries.14:10: A person who dies is gone, and no one knows where they are. It expresses the finality and mystery of death from a human viewpoint.
entries.14:11: Water drains from a pool and a river dries up. This picture shows how something can disappear completely and not come back.
entries.14:12: A person lies down in death and does not rise until the heavens end. It reflects the belief that the dead sleep and are not active.
entries.14:13: Job wishes God would hide him safely in the grave until his anger passes, then remember him at a set time. It is a longing for relief and a second chance.
entries.14:14: Job asks whether a dead person can live again, and says he would wait through all his hardship if release would come. It voices hope mixed with deep uncertainty.
entries.14:15: Job imagines God calling and him answering, and God longing for the work he made. It expresses a desire for restored relationship with God.
entries.14:16: Job feels God is counting his every step and not letting his sin go unnoticed. It conveys the feeling of being watched and held accountable.
entries.14:17: Job pictures his wrongdoing sealed up in a bag and his sin kept safe, meaning it is stored up and not forgotten. It shows his fear that his sins are being held against him.
entries.14:18: Mountains crumble and rocks shift from their place. This shows that even the most solid things in nature eventually break down.
entries.14:19: Water wears down stones and washes away soil, and in the same way God brings human hope to an end. It pictures how forces beyond our control can destroy what we count on.
entries.14:20: God overcomes a person permanently, and death changes their face and sends them away. It describes death as a final defeat that no one can resist.
entries.14:21: A dead person does not know whether their children are honored or humbled. It means death cuts people off from the ongoing life of their family.
entries.14:22: Even in death, the person's flesh still feels pain and their soul is sad. It expresses Job's sense that suffering does not simply stop at the grave.
entries.15:1: Eliphaz speaks up to answer Job. This is the start of his second speech to Job.
entries.15:2: Eliphaz asks whether a wise person would answer with empty talk that helps no one. He is saying Job's words are like hot air with no value.
entries.15:3: He asks whether anyone should argue using words that do no good. For the reader, it is a warning that talk without substance helps nobody.
entries.15:4: Eliphaz accuses Job of undermining respect for God and cutting short quiet worship. He claims Job's loud complaints are damaging his devotion to God.
entries.15:5: He says Job's own sin is driving what he says, and that he has learned to speak like a liar. In other words, Eliphaz thinks Job's words come from a bad heart.
entries.15:6: Eliphaz says he does not need to prove Job wrong, because Job's own words condemn him. The reader sees that words can testify against the one who speaks them.
entries.15:7: Eliphaz sarcastically asks if Job was the first person ever born or existed before the hills. He is mocking Job for acting as if he alone knows everything.
entries.15:8: He asks if Job sat in on God's private council and grabbed all wisdom for himself. The point is that no human has God's full knowledge.
entries.15:9: Eliphaz asks what Job knows that he and his friends do not. He is claiming they are just as wise as Job.
entries.15:10: He points to older, grey-haired men among them who are older than Job's father. He is saying age and tradition are on their side.
entries.15:11: Eliphaz asks whether God's comfort and gentle words are not enough for Job. He suggests Job is ignoring the kindness God has shown.
entries.15:12: He asks why Job's heart is out of control and his eyes look proud. He is accusing Job of arrogance and losing his temper.
entries.15:13: Eliphaz says Job is turning his spirit against God and letting angry words pour out. He sees Job's speech as rebellion against God.
entries.15:14: He asks how any human can be pure or upright. The point is that no person is perfectly clean before God.
entries.15:15: Eliphaz says God does not even trust his holy ones, and the heavens are not pure in his sight. He means that if even heavenly beings fall short, humans surely do.
entries.15:16: He says it is far worse for a person who is disgusting and unclean and drinks evil like water. The reader is meant to see how low Eliphaz thinks humans are.
entries.15:17: Eliphaz asks Job to listen, and says he will tell what he has seen. He is about to give his own observation as evidence.
entries.15:18: He says these are things wise men received from their fathers and did not hide. He is appealing to handed-down wisdom as reliable.
entries.15:19: He notes that the land was given only to those wise men, with no outsider among them. He is stressing that this teaching is pure and uncontaminated.
entries.15:20: Eliphaz claims the wicked suffer pain all their days and the cruel get only a few years. He is saying bad people always pay in this life.
entries.15:21: He says a wicked man hears sounds of terror, and destruction hits him even when things seem peaceful. The point is that the wicked never feel safe.
entries.15:22: He says the wicked have no hope of escaping the darkness, and the sword is waiting for them. Eliphaz is describing a doomed fate for evildoers.
entries.15:23: He pictures the wicked wandering around looking for bread and certain that trouble is coming. The reader sees a picture of constant anxiety.
entries.15:24: Eliphaz says fear of dark days overwhelms the wicked, and trouble and pain defeat him. He is saying the wicked live under constant dread.
entries.15:25: He explains this happens because the wicked shakes his fist at God and defies the Almighty. The suffering is presented as the result of proud rebellion.
entries.15:26: He describes the wicked charging at God like a soldier in heavy armor, like a king ready for battle. It pictures stubborn, defiant resistance to God.
entries.15:27: Eliphaz says the wicked man's face is covered with fat and his body has grown thick. He means the wicked lives in luxury and self-indulgence.
entries.15:28: He says the wicked settles in ruined towns and houses no one should live in, which are falling apart. The point is that his home is under judgment.
entries.15:29: He says the wicked will not get rich or keep what he has, and his crops will not flourish. Eliphaz claims prosperity will not last for the wicked.
entries.15:30: He says the wicked will not escape the darkness, and fire and wind will destroy his branches and buds. It is a picture of total loss.
entries.15:31: Eliphaz warns the wicked not to trust in what is false, because he will get deceit as his reward. The reader is warned that false hope pays back in disappointment.
entries.15:32: He says the wicked's branch is cut off before its time and its leaf stops being green. It means his life is cut short and loses its freshness.
entries.15:33: He compares the wicked to a vine whose grapes never ripen or an olive tree that drops its flowers. The point is that his life produces nothing good.
entries.15:34: Eliphaz says groups of evildoers bear no fruit, and the tents of those who take bribes will burn. He is saying corruption ends in ruin.
entries.15:35: He says evil people conceive trouble and give birth to it, and what comes from them is shame. The reader sees that sin produces its own bad results.
entries.16:1: Job speaks up again in reply to his friends. This simply marks the start of his answer to them.
entries.16:2: Job says he has heard this kind of talk many times before, and calls his friends comforters who only add to his pain. It reminds us that bad advice or harsh words can hurt more than help someone who is suffering.
entries.16:3: Job asks whether their endless windy speeches will ever stop, and what makes them keep arguing with him. He is pushing back against words that pile on instead of soothing.
entries.16:4: Job says he could easily talk the same way if their situations were swapped, and he could gang up on them with words and mocking gestures. He is pointing out how easy it is to criticize when you are not the one hurting.
entries.16:5: Job says that if he were in their place, he would use his words to strengthen them and offer real comfort. He is describing the kind of friend he wishes they had been to him.
entries.16:6: Job says that speaking his mind does not ease his pain, and staying silent does not make it go away either. He feels trapped with no way to find relief.
entries.16:7: Job says God has worn him out and left him gripped by trouble. He feels completely drained and overwhelmed by his suffering.
entries.16:8: Job says his own wasted body stands as evidence against him, as if his thinness testifies to his guilt. He feels that even his appearance is being used to accuse him.
entries.16:9: Job describes God as attacking him in anger, and says onlookers glare at him with cruelty. He feels surrounded by hostility from every side.
entries.16:10: Job says people open their mouths against him, strike him in the face with insults, and crowd together to oppose him. He feels ganged up on and humiliated.
entries.16:11: Job believes God has handed him over to wicked people and thrown him into their power. He feels abandoned to those who mean him harm.
entries.16:12: Job says he was once at ease, but God has shattered him, grabbed him by the neck, and set him up as a target. He feels his life has been turned from peace to being a bullseye.
entries.16:13: Job pictures attackers surrounding him and piercing him without mercy until his life drains away. He feels his suffering is relentless and deadly.
entries.16:14: Job says he is broken again and again, and that God charges at him like a warrior. He feels the blows keep coming with no letup.
entries.16:15: Job says he has worn rough sackcloth against his skin and laid his strength in the dust. These are outward signs of deep grief and humiliation.
entries.16:16: Job says his face is red from crying and his eyes grow dark. His grief is visible on his body and wearing him down.
entries.16:17: Job insists he has done nothing violent and that his prayer is sincere. He is claiming his suffering is not a fair punishment for wrongdoing.
entries.16:18: Job cries out that the earth should not hide his blood or silence his cry. He desperately wants his innocence and his suffering to be remembered and heard.
entries.16:19: Even now Job says his witness and defender is in heaven. In the middle of his pain he holds on to the hope that God above will speak for him.
entries.16:20: Job says his friends mock him while his eyes pour out tears to God. He feels misunderstood by people and turns his weeping toward God.
entries.16:21: Job longs for someone to argue his case with God, like a mediator between a person and God. He wants a fair hearing for his situation.
entries.16:22: Job says that soon he will set out on a journey from which he will not return, meaning death is near. He speaks as someone who feels his time is running short.
entries.17:1: Job feels completely crushed and believes his life is over, with nothing left but the grave. It means the reader should not be quick to judge someone who speaks this way in deep suffering.
entries.17:2: Job is surrounded by people who mock him, and their cruel laughter wears him down. It reminds the reader how much pain careless ridicule adds to someone already hurting.
entries.17:3: Job asks God himself to stand surety for him, because no human friend will take his side. It means when everyone else fails us, we can still bring our case directly to God.
entries.17:4: Job believes God has kept his accusers from understanding the truth, so they will not be honored. It means we should be careful about judging before we truly understand a situation.
entries.17:5: Job warns that a person who betrays a friend for personal gain brings trouble on his own family. It means loyalty matters, and betraying friends for profit has real consequences.
entries.17:6: Job has become a public joke, a byword and a target of mockery among the people. It shows how painful it is when a person's suffering becomes entertainment for others.
entries.17:7: Job's grief has drained his eyes and wasted his body until he is only a shadow. It means deep sorrow affects a person physically, not just emotionally.
entries.17:8: Good people are shocked and shaken when they see what is happening to Job. It means even the faithful can be disturbed when the innocent suffer.
entries.17:9: Despite everything, the upright person keeps going and grows stronger in doing right. It means hardship does not have to stop us from staying faithful.
entries.17:10: Job challenges his friends to come back, but says none of them has shown real wisdom. It means comforters who only criticize are not truly wise.
entries.17:11: Job feels his life is over and all his plans and hopes have been cut off. It means when plans collapse, it is honest to grieve what is lost.
entries.17:12: Job's friends keep insisting things will brighten, but he sees only darkness ahead. It means false optimism can feel like a denial of real pain.
entries.17:13: Job pictures death as his only home, with his bed made in darkness. It shows how completely hopeless he feels about his future.
entries.17:14: Job speaks of the grave and worms as his closest family, since death seems all he has left. It means he feels utterly abandoned by life itself.
entries.17:15: Job asks where his hope has gone and who will ever see what he longed for. It means when hope seems gone, the question of where to look next is real and painful.
entries.17:16: Job asks whether his hope will go down with him into the grave and the dust. It means he wonders if anything he hoped for can survive death.
entries.18:1: Bildad, one of Job's friends, speaks up next in the argument. He is about to give his own opinion about why Job is suffering.
entries.18:2: Bildad tells Job to stop talking so much and to listen and learn wisdom. He is frustrated that Job keeps defending himself instead of accepting their advice.
entries.18:3: Bildad feels insulted, as if Job treats him and his friends like stupid animals. He is saying Job is acting as though they know nothing.
entries.18:4: Bildad asks Job why the whole world should change just to suit him, and warns that Job is only hurting himself with his anger. He thinks Job is being unreasonable and self-centered.
entries.18:5: Bildad begins describing what he believes happens to wicked people: their success and happiness are snuffed out like a lamp. He is hinting that this is what has happened to Job.
entries.18:6: He pictures the wicked person's home going dark, with every source of light put out. In other words, trouble and ruin come to the wicked.
entries.18:7: The wicked person's strength fails and his own plans bring him down. Bildad is saying that evil people trip themselves up.
entries.18:8: He compares the wicked to someone who walks into a hidden trap without realizing it. Disaster catches them when they are not looking.
entries.18:9: The trap closes on the wicked person's foot and holds him fast. Bildad is saying that bad people cannot escape the consequences of their actions.
entries.18:10: A hidden snare waits in the path of the wicked person. Trouble is set up ahead of them, ready to catch them.
entries.18:11: The wicked person is surrounded by terrors that chase him at every step. Bildad describes a life of constant fear and dread.
entries.18:12: Hunger drains the wicked person's strength while disaster waits to strike him. His ruin is pictured as close and certain.
entries.18:13: Disease eats away the wicked person's skin and body. Bildad is describing sickness as part of the punishment that comes on evil people.
entries.18:14: The wicked person is dragged out of the safety of his home and brought to death, called here the king of fears. He loses everything he trusted in.
entries.18:15: Strangers take over the wicked person's home, and fire falls on his house. His property is destroyed and taken from him.
entries.18:16: The wicked person is like a plant whose roots dry up underground and whose branches are cut off above. Nothing of him is left growing or alive.
entries.18:17: The wicked person is forgotten completely, and no one remembers his name. His memory disappears from the world.
entries.18:18: He is driven out of the light into darkness and pushed out of the world. Bildad pictures total removal and disgrace.
entries.18:19: The wicked person has no children or family left among his people, and no one remains in his home to carry on his name. His family line comes to an end.
entries.18:20: People from east and west are shocked and terrified when they see what happened to the wicked person. His downfall becomes a warning to everyone.
entries.18:21: Bildad concludes that this is what happens to the homes of sinners and to those who ignore God. He is implying that Job's disaster proves Job is such a person.
entries.19:1: Job begins to speak again in response to his friends. This reminds the reader that he is still in the middle of the argument and is about to answer them directly.
entries.19:2: Job asks his friends how long they will keep hurting him and wearing him down with their words. It shows how much their constant criticism has hurt him.
entries.19:3: Job says they have insulted him many times and feel no shame about treating him badly. The reader sees that repeated harsh words do real damage.
entries.19:4: Job says that if he really has done something wrong, it only affects him, not them. He is pushing back on their claim to be his judges.
entries.19:5: Job points out that they are acting superior to him and using his suffering as proof he is guilty. It warns against assuming someone's pain means they did wrong.
entries.19:6: Job insists that it is God who has treated him unfairly and trapped him like an animal in a net. He is honest about feeling that God is against him.
entries.19:7: Job cries out that violence is being done to him, but no one answers or defends him. It shows the pain of calling for help and getting silence.
entries.19:8: Job says God has blocked his path and made his road dark so he cannot move forward. He feels trapped with no way out.
entries.19:9: Job says God has stripped him of his honor and taken away his dignity. He has lost the respect and standing he once had.
entries.19:10: Job feels broken down on every side and says his hope has been pulled up like a dead tree. It pictures total collapse and loss of hope.
entries.19:11: Job believes God's anger is burning against him and treats him like an enemy. He is expressing how personal and painful this feels.
entries.19:12: Job describes God's forces closing in on him like an army surrounding his tent. He feels completely besieged and helpless.
entries.19:13: Job says God has pushed his brothers far away, and they now treat him like a stranger. Suffering has left him isolated even from family.
entries.19:14: Job's relatives and close friends have abandoned him, and even his household has forgotten him. It shows how quickly people can disappear when someone suffers.
entries.19:15: Job says even his servants treat him like a foreigner. He has lost his place and status in his own home.
entries.19:16: Job calls his servant but gets no answer, and has to beg him for attention. It shows how far his authority and dignity have fallen.
entries.19:17: Job says his breath is offensive to his wife and he is repulsive to his own family. His suffering has made even those closest to him pull away.
entries.19:18: Job says even young children disrespect him and turn their backs when he stands up. He feels mocked by everyone, even the least expected.
entries.19:19: Job says all his close companions avoid him and those he loved have turned against him. It shows the deep loneliness of being rejected by friends.
entries.19:20: Job describes himself as skin and bones, barely escaping with his life. It pictures how severe and wasting his suffering has become.
entries.19:21: Job begs his friends to show him pity because God's hand has come down hard on him. He asks for compassion instead of more judgment.
entries.19:22: Job asks why his friends are cruel to him, as if they were God, and keep speaking against him. He is hurt that they pile on more pain.
entries.19:23: Job wishes his words could be written down and recorded. He wants his side of the story to be preserved.
entries.19:24: Job wishes his words were carved into rock with iron and lead so they would last forever. It shows how much he wants his complaint remembered.
entries.19:25: Even in the worst loss, Job says his Redeemer lives. Hope can stand up in the middle of grief.
entries.19:26: Even after his body is destroyed, Job expects to see God. This is a striking statement of hope beyond his suffering.
entries.19:27: Job says he will see God for himself, not as a stranger, and his heart longs for it. It shows a deep personal hope of meeting God.
entries.19:28: Job warns that if they claim he is being punished because sin is at his root, they are wrong. He is defending himself against their accusations.
entries.19:29: Job warns them to fear the sword of judgment, because there is a judge who sees what they are doing. It is a reminder that God will hold people accountable for how they treat others.
entries.20:1: Zophar speaks up next in the argument. He is one of Job's friends who thinks he knows why Job is suffering.
entries.20:2: Zophar says his thoughts are restless and pushing him to answer. He feels he has to speak up because he is upset.
entries.20:3: Zophar says Job's words insult him and are just empty talk. He is offended and thinks Job's answers make no sense.
entries.20:4: Zophar asks if Job knows what has been true since people were first put on earth. He appeals to old, common wisdom.
entries.20:5: Zophar claims that a wicked person's pride and happiness only last a short time. He is saying that evil people always get cut down quickly.
entries.20:6: Even if a wicked person rises very high and seems great, it will not last. Zophar pictures someone lifted up to the sky.
entries.20:7: The wicked person will vanish forever like dung that is thrown away. People who saw him will wonder where he went.
entries.20:8: He will disappear like a dream you forget when you wake up. He will be gone like a vision in the night that leaves nothing behind.
entries.20:9: No one will see him again, and the place where he lived will not remember him. He will be completely forgotten.
entries.20:10: His children will have to beg from the poor, and he will have to give back the wealth he took. His family will suffer for his wrongs.
entries.20:11: His body is full of youthful strength now, but it will die and turn to dust with him. His energy will not save him from death.
entries.20:12: Even though doing evil tastes sweet to him and he hides it in his mouth like a treat. He enjoys his sin and keeps it secret.
entries.20:13: He holds on to his evil and refuses to let it go. He keeps it close because he likes it.
entries.20:14: But that sweet evil turns bitter in his stomach and becomes like snake poison inside him. What he enjoyed ends up hurting him.
entries.20:15: He swallows down wealth, but God makes him vomit it back up. He cannot keep what he gained by doing wrong.
entries.20:16: He drinks in snake poison, and it kills him. The evil he took in destroys him.
entries.20:17: He will never enjoy the good things of life, like streams of honey and milk. His wrongdoing cuts him off from blessings.
entries.20:18: He has to give back what he worked for and cannot enjoy it. He gets no pleasure from his profits.
entries.20:19: He did this because he was cruel to the poor and ignored them when they were in trouble. He also took houses by force that he did not build.
entries.20:20: His wealth gives him no peace, and the things he loved cannot save him. He is restless and unsafe.
entries.20:21: He was never satisfied with what he had. Because of his greed, his good times will end quickly.
entries.20:22: Even when he is rich, he is full of worry because everyone in trouble turns against him. His abundance brings him anxiety, not safety.
entries.20:23: God gives him what he wants, but then pours out his anger on him like rain. His desires become the doorway to judgment.
entries.20:24: He may run from an iron weapon, but a bronze arrow will strike him. There is no escape from the danger coming for him.
entries.20:25: The arrow goes through his body, and he is overcome with fear. He is struck down and terrified.
entries.20:26: Darkness is kept for all his wealth, and a fire not made by human hands destroys him and everything in his tent. Total ruin comes on him and his home.
entries.20:27: The heavens reveal his sin, and the earth itself testifies against him. His wrongdoing is exposed and cannot be hidden.
entries.20:28: His household's goods are carried off to another land, taken away on the day of wrath. His family loses everything.
entries.20:29: This is what Zophar says the wicked receive from God. He believes this is the fate God gives to evil people.
entries.21:1: Job speaks up in reply to his friends. He is about to answer what they have said to him.
entries.21:2: Job asks his friends to listen closely to what he is saying. He says that simply listening would be a real comfort to him.
entries.21:3: Job wants a chance to speak his mind without being interrupted. After that, he says, they can mock him if they want.
entries.21:4: Job asks whether his complaint is really aimed at people. If his spirit is troubled, he feels he has good reason for it.
entries.21:5: Job tells them to look at him and be shocked. He wants them to cover their mouths in silence rather than keep arguing.
entries.21:6: Just thinking about his situation makes Job's body tremble with fear. His distress is deep and physical, not just words.
entries.21:7: Job asks a hard question: why do wicked people often live long and grow powerful? It bothers him that bad people seem to do well.
entries.21:8: The wicked see their children grow up around them. Their families stay close and thrive before their eyes.
entries.21:9: Their homes are safe and free from fear. They don't seem to suffer the punishment God is supposed to bring.
entries.21:10: Even their farm animals prosper. Their cattle breed successfully and don't lose their young.
entries.21:11: Their children run around happily like a flock of sheep. The young ones play and dance together.
entries.21:12: They sing and celebrate to music. They enjoy life and are glad when they hear instruments playing.
