entries.40:20: The mountains provide its food, where other wild animals play. It shows God providing for even the biggest and strangest creatures.
entries.40:21: It rests under shady trees by the river and pools. It pictures a calm, strong creature living safely in the wild.
entries.40:22: Trees and river grasses cover and surround it. It shows how at home this huge beast is in God's creation.
entries.40:23: Even a flooding river does not scare it, and it stays calm when the Jordan rushes at it. It shows a creature so strong it fears nothing, a picture of power God made.
entries.40:24: God asks whether anyone can catch it while it watches or put a hook through its nose. It shows that no human can tame what God has made.
entries.41:1: God asks Job whether a person could catch this huge sea monster with a simple fishhook. The point is that some things are far too powerful for us to control.
entries.41:2: God asks if Job could lead this beast around with a rope through its nose or tongue. It means we cannot tame or manage what is beyond our strength.
entries.41:3: God asks whether the monster would beg for mercy or speak gently to get free. The answer is no, showing it fears no one.
entries.41:4: God asks if the beast would make a deal to become a servant forever. It cannot be bargained with or owned by a person.
entries.41:5: God asks if Job could treat it like a pet bird or put it on a leash for young girls. Such a creature is not a plaything.
entries.41:6: God asks if fishermen could sell it or cut it up for traders. It is not something people can profit from.
entries.41:7: God asks if Job could pierce its hide with sharp irons or spears. Ordinary weapons cannot hurt it.
entries.41:8: God tells Job to just try laying a hand on it once and see the fight he would get. He would never want to try again.
entries.41:9: Anyone who hopes to beat this creature is fooling himself; just seeing it is enough to defeat a person.
entries.41:10: The beast is so fierce that no one dares to stir it up. So how could anyone stand against God, who made it?
entries.41:11: God says no one has ever given to him first or defeated him, since everything under heaven belongs to him.
entries.41:12: God says he will not stay silent about the monster's body, its power, and its strong build.
entries.41:13: God asks who could strip off its outer skin or get past its inner armor. No one can.
entries.41:14: God asks who could force open its jaws, which are ringed with terrifying teeth.
entries.41:15: Its back is covered with rows of tight-fitting plates, pressed together like a seal.
entries.41:16: The plates fit so closely that no air can get between them.
entries.41:17: They grip each other and are joined so firmly they cannot be pulled apart.
entries.41:18: Its sneezes flash like fire, and its eyes look like the first light of dawn.
entries.41:19: Fire and flames come out of its mouth.
entries.41:20: Smoke pours from its nose like steam from a boiling pot.
entries.41:21: Its breath can set coals ablaze, and flame comes from its mouth.
entries.41:22: Great strength is in its neck, and terror goes ahead of it.
entries.41:23: The folds of its flesh are firm and fixed, impossible to move.
entries.41:24: Its heart is as hard as stone, like the heavy stone used for grinding grain.
entries.41:25: When it rises to fight, even strong warriors are overcome with fear.
entries.41:26: Swords, spears, arrows, and sharp iron cannot pierce it.
entries.41:27: It treats iron like straw and bronze like soft wood.
entries.41:28: Arrows cannot make it run, and stones mean no more to it than dry grass.
entries.41:29: A club is like a blade of grass to it, and it laughs at the charge of a spear.
entries.41:30: Its belly is like sharp broken pottery, and it drags through the mud like a threshing tool.
entries.41:31: It churns the deep water like a boiling pot and stirs the sea like perfume being mixed.
entries.41:32: It leaves a shining trail behind it, making the deep water look white.
entries.41:33: There is nothing else on earth like it, a creature made without fear.
entries.41:34: It looks down on everything proud and tall, and it rules over all the proud beasts.
entries.42:1: Job begins his reply to God after God has spoken to him out of the storm. He is about to admit that he was wrong to question God.
entries.42:2: Job admits that God can do anything and that no plan of his can be blocked. For the reader, this means God's power and purposes are never defeated.
entries.42:3: Job repeats God's question and admits he spoke about things too wonderful for him to understand. It reminds us to be humble when we talk about God's ways.
entries.42:4: Job asks God to listen while he speaks and to answer his questions. He is inviting God to respond directly to him.
entries.42:5: Before this, Job had only heard about God, but now he has encountered him personally. It shows that knowing about God is not the same as truly meeting him.
entries.42:6: Job takes back what he said and humbly repents, sitting in dust and ashes as a sign of sorrow. It teaches that real repentance means admitting we were wrong.
entries.42:7: God tells Eliphaz and his friends that he is angry because they did not speak the truth about him, while Job did. It warns that saying wrong things about God matters.
entries.42:8: God tells the friends to bring sacrifices and have Job pray for them so they will not be punished. It shows God's mercy and that he listens to the prayers of a faithful person.
entries.42:9: The three friends obey God and do what he commanded, and God accepts Job's prayer for them. It shows that obedience brings God's favor and that he hears prayer.
entries.42:10: After Job prayed for his friends, God restored his fortunes and gave him twice as much as he had before. It shows that blessing came after Job forgave and prayed for those who had hurt him.
entries.42:11: Job's family and old friends come to comfort him and bring him gifts of money and gold. It shows that God's restoration included the support of people around him.
entries.42:12: God blessed the later part of Job's life even more than the beginning, with huge numbers of animals. It shows that God can restore and multiply what was lost.
entries.42:13: Job again has seven sons and three daughters. His family is restored after his great loss.
entries.42:14: Job names his three daughters Jemimah, Keziah, and Keren-happuch. Naming them shows they were precious to him and part of his restored joy.
entries.42:15: Job's daughters were the most beautiful women in the land, and he gave them an inheritance along with their brothers. This was unusual for the time and shows Job's generosity and care for his daughters.
entries.42:16: Job lives another hundred and forty years and sees his descendants down to the fourth generation. It shows God's blessing of long life and family continuing.
entries.42:17: Job dies at a good old age, having lived a full life. It shows that his story ends in peace and honor rather than in suffering.
